notes:
CHRISTIANITY - THE WAY OF JESUS CHRIST

OPENING QUOTES
- John 14:6-7: Jesus said, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you know me, you will know my Father also.'
- MONIKA HELLWIG describes the original experience of Jesus: ordinary people were attracted to a wandering preacher who spoke in towns, villages and the countryside.
- His message called them back to the hope their religious traditions in Israel gave them, and to trust and confidence in God.
- He spoke in ordinary language. He showed God's presence and care by his own human presence and care for others, his way of living, his values and priorities, his prayer and how he related to people.
- In him people found new life, hope, challenge, purpose in life and healing.

THE GROWTH OF THE CHRISTIAN CHURCH
- The history of the Christian community spans two thousand years. It is a community of love, worship and service, rooted in the mystery of God's presence.
- PENTECOST: the gift of the Holy Spirit transformed the fear-filled, dejected apostles and disciples.
- ST PETER began preaching about Jesus the Christ on Pentecost Sunday, testifying to all God had done in Jesus of Nazareth.
- ST LUKE, author of the ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, records that over three thousand believed and were baptised.
- Acts 2-15 describes the young Church: preaching, praying, caring for the needy, fellowship, meals and baptising, while leadership structures developed amid persecution.

GAMALIEL'S ADVICE
- Many early converts were Jews, so the SADDUCEES (priests of the Temple) were alarmed and wanted to suppress the community.
- GAMALIEL, a famous first-century rabbi, advised (Acts 5:38-39): leave these men alone; 'if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them' - you may even be found fighting against God.

THE EARLY CHURCH
- Most early Christians were Jews who still went to synagogues and followed the Jewish way of life.
- As the community grew, Greek influences appeared in its teaching and symbols.
- The early Church was a collection of small communities who believed the end of the world was imminent (very near). They saw themselves living under God's rule, guided by Jesus' message.
- Over time structures developed: BISHOPS, ELDERS and DEACONS organised the growing churches.
- Many Jewish Christians felt threatened, left Jerusalem and preached in surrounding territories. So the message reached non-Jews, called GENTILES - an important element in the spread of Christianity.

ST PAUL AND THE COUNCIL OF JERUSALEM (50 CE)
- St Paul is the central figure in this New Testament story.
- In 50 CE a debate arose in Jerusalem about the external rituals of Jewish Christians: circumcision, ritual washing and dietary laws.
- Paul emphasised: 'What makes a person righteous is not obedience to the Law but faith in Jesus Christ' (Galatians 2:16).
- From then on converts did not have to observe Jewish rituals.

PERSECUTION AND ACCEPTANCE
- Horrific persecutions began under EMPEROR NERO (38-68 CE) and continued in waves under DOMITIAN, MARCUS AURELIUS and DIOCLETIAN (three of the most severe).
- Despite this, the communities grew in numbers and influence in the Roman Empire.
- The early Church saw itself as the BODY OF CHRIST: every member had a role - to be a sign of God's love, to minister and preach, to support one another in crisis.
- Persecution generally stopped from 312 CE, when CONSTANTINE became emperor.
- In the fourth century Christianity became more formalised; by 381 it was the official religion of the Roman Empire.

VISION OF SALVATION
- CHRIST/MESSIAH: Christians believe Jesus is the Messiah. In Old Testament times kings and priests were anointed with oil to show God chose them; the spirit of the Lord worked through these anointed ones for the people. 'Messiah' (Hebrew) and 'Christ' (Greek) both mean 'the anointed One'.
- RESURRECTION: Christians believe all Jesus said and did was vindicated (shown to be right) and accepted by God in raising him from the dead.
- At Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:13-17, Mark 1:9-11, Luke 3:21-22) a voice from heaven said: 'You are my son, the beloved, my favour rests on you.'
- The Resurrection shows the Father's approval of Jesus' life and death. Christians model their lives on Jesus, hoping for triumph over death and eternal life.
- The phrase 'JESUS IS LORD' sums up all Christians believe about the Resurrection.
- REDEMPTION: Christianity is a religion of redemption. When we turn away from sin (wrongdoing) and accept God's forgiveness through Jesus, the Spirit of the Lord is with us again. God sent Jesus to redeem people who had turned away. God takes the initiative; the Church responds.
- SALVATION: Christianity is a religion of salvation. Jesus' life, death and resurrection offer all who believe a special relationship with God.
- SIN: the human failure to do God's will and to live by kingdom standards, that is, by love. Sin is overcome by Jesus' victory over evil and death.
- Christians believe Christ will judge the world at the end of time; through this saving action Christians will be blessed with eternal happiness (heaven).
- John 3:16: 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.'

A COMMUNITY OF BELIEVERS - MANY CHRISTIAN FAMILIES, ONE SAVING CHRIST
- Like a tree with many branches, Christianity has many DENOMINATIONAL GROUPS. Their common root is the Good News of Jesus of Nazareth, their first-century Jewish founder.
- THREE MAIN BRANCHES: Roman Catholicism, Eastern Orthodox and Protestantism. Many others are grouped as Pentecostal/Evangelical.
- Each has its own living tradition with strong structures of ministry and authority.
- Unity within diversity is a sign that the gospel is good news for all.
- THE ECUMENICAL MOVEMENT encourages traditions to keep their distinctiveness but also work together in prayer, preaching, service and community.

ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH
- The largest Christian church.
- Hierarchical: headed by the POPE of Rome as successor of St Peter, with bishops worldwide as successors of the apostles.
- Only celibate males may become priests and bishops.
- Since VATICAN COUNCIL II there has been a move away from stressing hierarchy towards seeing the Church as the PEOPLE OF GOD - a community united by faith in Jesus and joined by baptism.

EASTERN ORTHODOX CHURCHES
- Arose from a split in 1054 between the Bishop of Rome and the Eastern churches of Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem, after centuries of drifting apart.
- Orthodox priests may marry, but bishops are typically celibate.
- The DIVINE LITURGY is the most important service.
- Ancient mystical tradition of liturgy and prayer using ICONS as objects of veneration in community and personal prayer.

PROTESTANT CHURCHES
- Many churches, varying in theology, liturgy and size. Their uniting factor is a historical period which saw the growth of nationalism and capitalism.
- Main Protestant churches: Anglicanism, Lutheran and Calvinist churches, Presbyterianism, the Religious Society of Friends, and the Baptist Church.
- Some, like the Anglican Communion, ordain women as priests and bishops; others do not.
- Priests and bishops do not have to be celibate.
- They often define themselves against Catholicism: rejecting the primacy and infallibility of the Pope and having a different understanding of the sacraments.
- Positively, they share with Catholics the centrality of scripture in guiding Christian living and each individual's responsibility to work towards salvation, guided by scripture.

PENTECOSTAL/EVANGELICAL CHRISTIANS
- A large group of separate churches, linked by how their pastor/minister/leader preaches with raw emotion, relying on the power of the Spirit to invigorate lives, cure sickness and banish evil.
- Worship is informal: powerful preaching and rhythmic singing. Speaking in tongues and prophetic sermons are regular features.
- The movement began in the USA as a reaction to formal styles of worship.
- Fast-growing, with over 100 million followers worldwide.

COMMUNITY IN CHRISTIANITY
- For all Christian families community is central: following Christ means active community life of fellowship, prayer and service.
- The true call: love God above all things and love your neighbour as yourself. The community is Spirit-inspired and driven.
- FR NIALL O'BRIEN, a Columban mission priest, in 'No Christianity without Community': lay participation is not just lay people doing liturgical acts; it is a commitment to building a believing, sharing community that looks after the poor and speaks out for justice - an evangelising community.
- SOURCES OF AUTHORITY: inspired scripture, shared experience and tradition (including church documents and councils), and the ordained hierarchy (bishops). Churches differ in which they stress, giving different understandings of priesthood, ministry and structure.
- Unifying factor: the challenge to live by gospel standards and build God's kingdom in a changing world.

TAIZE
- A Christian community in eastern France - a shining example of community living rising above denominational differences. Linked with BROTHER ROGER.
- Key theme: RECONCILIATION. People of all backgrounds gather in prayer and community.
- Visitors meditate on: 'You have come to Taize to find a meaning to your life. One of Christ's secrets is that he loved you first... to be loved forever, to be clothed with God's forgiveness and trust, as if by a garment. In this way you will be able to take the risk of giving your life.'

A CELEBRATING TRADITION - BAPTISM
- Christians are initiated (joined) into the Church through Baptism.
- Main symbol: WATER, representing life and cleansing.
- Churches differ in how they celebrate it, but all agree it involves: renouncing sin; dying to the old way of life; starting a new life in Christ; receiving the Holy Spirit.

EUCHARIST / HOLY COMMUNION
- The other sacrament common to most Christians.
- Two main parts: (1) readings, prayers and homily/sermon; (2) the liturgy of the Eucharist, whose symbolic action is a MEAL and a SACRIFICE.
- Churches celebrate it at different frequencies: every day, weekly, six times a year or less.
- It involves: the presence of Christ; the unity of believers with one another; the sacrificial death of Christ; memorial and covenant.

THE SEVEN SACRAMENTS OF THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH
- Sacrament: a symbolic word, gesture or object that makes a hidden reality visible.
- SACRAMENTS OF INITIATION: Baptism (new life, belonging to Christ and his Church); Eucharist (presence of Christ with the community); Confirmation (full, committed discipleship; full membership rights and obligations).
- SACRAMENTS OF HEALING: Reconciliation (conversion and forgiveness); Anointing of the Sick (strengthening and support).
- SACRAMENTS OF VOCATION: Marriage (lifelong loving commitment); Holy Orders/ordination (service and guidance).

WORSHIP AND FUNERALS
- SUNDAY, the day of Resurrection, is the central day for public worship. Public and private prayer both matter; Sunday worship in scripture and sacrament is the high point of the week.
- In funeral rites the community focuses on the promise of salvation, life after death and eternal rest in heaven.

CHRISTIAN FESTIVALS
- Three groupings: (1) those following the LUNAR cycle - Lent, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost; (2) those set by the SOLAR calendar - Christmas; (3) the annual cycle of feast days of saints and martyrs.
- LENT: seven weeks of penance and fasting preparing for Easter. It ends with HOLY WEEK, the seven days before Easter Sunday, remembering the last events of Jesus' life: the Last Supper, the arrest in the Garden of Gethsemane, the trial and crucifixion - with solemn rituals of service, mourning and penance.
- EASTER: the central festival - joy that Jesus is risen. The Easter vigil of prayer, ritual and Eucharist is richly symbolic. Easter is the festival of resurrection, of triumph over sin and death - the most important festival of the year for all Christians.
- ASCENSION DAY: forty days after Easter Sunday; celebrates Christ's ascension to heaven.
- PENTECOST: recalls the disciples receiving the Spirit and the power and courage to preach. Considered the BIRTHDAY OF THE CHURCH.
- ADVENT: four weeks preparing for Christmas, focusing on Christ's future return as Lord. Chant: 'Maranatha, come Lord Jesus'.
- CHRISTMAS: 25 December for most Christians; celebrates Jesus' birth. Once the date of an ancient Roman sun festival, transformed to celebrate the Prince of Peace, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, Light of the World.
- Poem 'Christmas is Really for the Children' by STEVE TURNER contrasts gentle Christmas images with the harsh events of Easter.

CHALLENGES TO THE TRADITION
- Daily challenge: witnessing to the values of its founder; helping people encounter Christ and live gospel values. Three big areas of (often bitter) debate:
- 1. SOCIAL JUSTICE: balancing public opposition to oppressive social and political structures with ministry to individuals. ARCHBISHOP OSCAR ROMERO (martyred): 'it is not God's will for some to have everything and others to have nothing... God's will is that all his children be happy.' If the Church sides with the rich and powerful it loses credibility; 'the servant church is losing contact with its servant king'.
- 2. RELIGIOUS PLURALISM and INTER-FAITH DIALOGUE: relations with other religions and the question of salvation outside the Church. HANS KUNG (Catholic theologian) says Judaism, Christianity and Islam have far more in common than divides them: all are religions of faith in the one God (Arab Christians also call God Allah); all have a historical stamp, looking to a consummation of the world rather than cosmic cycles; all were shaped by great prophetic figures (prophetic, not mystical); all have Holy Scriptures ('religions of the book'); all share a basic ethic of great commandments.
- 3. GENDER EQUALITY AND SEXUALITY: ordination of women, same-sex unions, birth control, abuse of children, the worldwide AIDS crisis - guiding the faithful without compromising the gospel.
- CONCLUSION: the Church is only credible when judged by gospel standards. 'The gospel is its challenge. The gospel is its inspiration. The gospel is its promise and fulfilment.'

KEY TERMS
- Community, Pentecost, Messiah, Resurrection, Redemption, Salvation, Denominational groups, Roman Catholic Church, Eastern Orthodox churches, Pentecostal/Evangelical Christians, Protestant churches, God's kingdom, Sacrament, Eucharist, Easter, Christmas.

rows.prompt: Describe the life of the young Church as recorded in Acts 2-15.
rows.model_answer: The young Church was a life of preaching, praying, caring for the needy, fellowship, sharing meals and baptising. Structures of leadership developed while the community endured persecution. Over time bishops, elders and deacons organised the growing churches.

rows.prompt: Explain the importance of St Paul in the spread of Christianity.
rows.model_answer: Paul is the central figure in the spread of the message to the Gentiles. At the debate in Jerusalem in 50 CE about circumcision, ritual washing and dietary laws, he argued that faith in Jesus Christ, not obedience to the Law, makes a person righteous (Galatians 2:16). After this, converts did not have to keep Jewish rituals, which opened Christianity to non-Jews.

rows.prompt: What do Christians believe about the Resurrection?
rows.model_answer: Christians believe God raised Jesus from the dead, showing that everything he said and did was accepted by God. It shows the Father's approval of Jesus' life and death. Christians model their lives on Jesus in hope of triumph over death and eternal life, summed up in the phrase 'Jesus is Lord'.

rows.prompt: Name the three main branches of Christianity and give one feature of each.
rows.model_answer: Roman Catholicism is the largest church, headed by the Pope as successor of St Peter. Eastern Orthodoxy came from the split of 1054; its priests may marry and it uses icons in prayer, with the Divine Liturgy as its main service. Protestant churches, such as the Anglican, Lutheran and Presbyterian churches, reject the primacy of the Pope and do not require clergy to be celibate.

rows.prompt: Write a short note on Pentecostal/Evangelical Christians.
rows.model_answer: They are a large group of separate churches whose leaders preach with raw emotion, relying on the power of the Spirit to cure sickness and banish evil. Worship is informal, with powerful preaching, rhythmic singing, speaking in tongues and prophetic sermons. The movement began in the USA as a reaction to formal worship and has over 100 million followers.

rows.prompt: Name the four elements that all churches say Baptism involves.
rows.model_answer: Baptism involves renouncing sin, dying to the old way of life, starting a new life in Christ and receiving the Holy Spirit. Its main symbol is water, which represents life and cleansing.

rows.prompt: Name the seven Catholic sacraments in their three groups.
rows.model_answer: The sacraments of initiation are Baptism, Eucharist and Confirmation. The sacraments of healing are Reconciliation and Anointing of the Sick. The sacraments of vocation are Marriage and Holy Orders.

rows.prompt: What did Archbishop Oscar Romero say about poverty and God's will?
rows.model_answer: Romero said many would like the poor to believe it is God's will for them to live that way, but it is not God's will for some to have everything and others nothing. God's will is that all his children be happy. The chapter warns that if the Church sides with the rich and powerful it loses credibility.

rows.prompt: Outline the vision of salvation proposed by Christianity.
rows.model_answer:
Christianity is a religion of redemption and salvation centred on Jesus. Christians believe Jesus is the Messiah or Christ, which means 'the anointed One'. In the Old Testament, kings and priests were anointed with oil to show God chose them, and the spirit of the Lord worked through them for the people.

At Jesus' baptism a voice from heaven said, 'You are my son, the beloved, my favour rests on you.' Christians believe that God accepted everything Jesus said and did by raising him from the dead. The Resurrection shows the Father's approval, and the phrase 'Jesus is Lord' sums up this belief.

Sin is the human failure to do God's will and to live by love. God took the initiative and sent Jesus to redeem people who had turned away. When people turn from sin and accept God's forgiveness through Jesus, the Spirit of the Lord is with them again. Jesus' victory over evil and death overcomes sin, and his life, death and resurrection offer everyone who believes a special relationship with God. Christians believe Christ will judge the world at the end of time and that believers will receive eternal happiness in heaven. As John 3:16 says, 'God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.'
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Messiah/Christ = anointed One and Old Testament anointing; baptism voice; Resurrection as God's vindication, 'Jesus is Lord'; redemption - turning from sin, God takes initiative; sin defined; salvation - relationship with God, victory over evil and death; judgement and heaven; John 3:16.

rows.prompt: Describe how the Christian Church grew in its first four centuries.
rows.model_answer:
At Pentecost the Holy Spirit transformed the fearful apostles. St Peter preached about Jesus and, according to St Luke in Acts, over three thousand were baptised. The young Church prayed, preached, cared for the needy, shared meals and baptised. When the Sadducees wanted to suppress it, the rabbi Gamaliel advised leaving the Christians alone: if the movement was of God it could not be overthrown.

Most early Christians were Jews who still went to the synagogue, but Greek influences grew. Communities believed the end of the world was near, and bishops, elders and deacons were set up to organise them. Many Jewish Christians left Jerusalem and preached to the Gentiles. St Paul was central: at Jerusalem in 50 CE he argued that faith in Jesus Christ, not obedience to the Law, makes a person righteous, so converts no longer had to keep circumcision or dietary laws.

Cruel persecution began under Nero and continued under Domitian, Marcus Aurelius and Diocletian, yet the Church grew, seeing itself as the Body of Christ. Persecution generally ended in 312 CE when Constantine became emperor, and by 381 Christianity was the official religion of the Roman Empire.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Pentecost and Peter's preaching; 3,000 baptised; life in Acts 2-15; Gamaliel; Jewish roots and Greek influence; bishops, elders, deacons; Gentiles; Paul and the 50 CE debate (Galatians 2:16); persecution under Nero and others; Body of Christ; Constantine 312; official religion 381. Credit accurate dates and names.

rows.prompt: Christianity is like a tree with many branches. Describe two of the main branches of Christianity.
rows.model_answer:
The Roman Catholic Church is the largest Christian church. It is hierarchical, headed by the Pope of Rome as successor of St Peter, with bishops worldwide as successors of the apostles. Only celibate men may be priests and bishops. Since Vatican Council II it has moved away from stressing hierarchy and sees itself as the People of God, a community united by faith in Jesus Christ and joined by baptism.

The Eastern Orthodox churches came from the split in 1054 between the Bishop of Rome and the Eastern churches of Constantinople, Antioch, Alexandria and Jerusalem, after centuries of drifting apart. Orthodox priests may marry, though bishops are usually celibate. The Divine Liturgy is the most important service, and there is an ancient mystical tradition of liturgy and prayer using icons as objects of veneration.

Both share the common root of all Christian families: the Good News of Jesus of Nazareth.
rows.marking_scheme: Name two branches 2 marks (1+1). Description 4 marks each (key facts: leadership/authority, origin, clergy rules, worship). Protestant (rejects papal primacy, no celibacy rule, some ordain women, centrality of scripture) or Pentecostal (emotional preaching, tongues, began in USA, 100 million) also accepted.

rows.prompt: Discuss two major challenges facing Christianity today.
rows.model_answer:
The first challenge is social justice. Christians must balance public opposition to oppressive social and political structures with ministry to individuals and groups. Archbishop Oscar Romero, who was martyred, said it is not God's will for some to have everything and others nothing; God's will is that all his children be happy. If the Church is seen to side with the rich and powerful, it loses credibility, because Christ challenged injustice and reached out to the poor and rejected. In the chapter's words, 'the servant church is losing contact with its servant king'.

The second challenge is religious pluralism and inter-faith dialogue, including the question of salvation outside the Church. The theologian Hans Kung argues that Judaism, Christianity and Islam have far more in common than divides them: all believe in one God (Arab Christians also call God Allah), all have a historical view looking to a consummation of the world, all were shaped by great prophets, all have Holy Scriptures, and all share a basic ethic of great commandments.

A third area is gender and sexuality, such as women's ordination and same-sex unions. The chapter concludes that the Church is only credible when judged by gospel standards.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Two challenges x 10 marks (name 2 + explanation with evidence 8). May refer to: social justice and Romero quote, credibility, servant church; religious pluralism, salvation outside the Church, Hans Kung's five shared features; gender equality and sexuality (ordination of women, same-sex unions, birth control, child abuse, AIDS); gospel as the standard.
